ai.definition: Neural uploads involve the transfer of a human brain's cognitive functions into a digital format. This process aims to preserve or replicate a person's consciousness in a computer system.
ai.howItWorks: The technology involves mapping the intricate neural connections and patterns within the brain, followed by replicating these structures in a digital environment. Techniques may include invasive implants that record neural activity and non-invasive methods like advanced MRI scans.
ai.problemSolved: Neural uploads address the challenge of preserving human consciousness beyond physical death or for long-term storage and analysis of cognitive functions.
ai.manufacturing: Current technology is not capable of performing such a transfer. The necessary hardware and software are in development stages, with significant challenges remaining in data fidelity and ethical considerations.
ai.buildProcess: The build process involves developing highly advanced neuroimaging techniques, creating detailed models of neural networks, and integrating these into a robust digital environment that can simulate cognitive functions accurately.
ai.costDrivers: High costs stem from the need for cutting-edge neuroscience research, specialized hardware development, and ethical and legal compliance. The cost is currently speculative but could be exorbitant due to the complexity involved.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The technology is in an early conceptual phase with significant hurdles to overcome before becoming viable. It may take decades of research and development to achieve practical applications.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks are non-existent, making it difficult to manage the ethical, legal, and safety implications of such a technology. Current discussions focus on theoretical scenarios rather than concrete policies.
ai.risks: Risks include data loss during transfer, irreversible damage to the original brain, security breaches in digital storage, and potential misuse of the technology for unethical purposes.
ai.profitability: Profitability is uncertain due to the speculative nature of the technology. If successful, it could revolutionize industries like healthcare, entertainment, and data storage but would require significant investment and time.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development will likely focus on improving neuroimaging techniques, enhancing computational models of neural networks, and addressing ethical concerns through international cooperation and policy-making.

glossary.def: The intricate network of neurons and synapses in the brain that form the basis for cognitive functions.
The accuracy with which digital representations match real-world neural activities, crucial for successful neural uploads.
Devices inserted into the brain to record and transmit neural activity directly.
Techniques that do not require physical insertion of devices, such as advanced MRI or EEG, used for mapping brain activity.

subsystems.name: Preservation and preparation
subsystems.role: stabilise a brain so its finest structure survives the scanning process.

subsystems.name: Volumetric imaging
subsystems.role: image every neuron and synapse at nanometre resolution.

subsystems.name: Connectome reconstruction
subsystems.role: turn petabytes of images into a wiring diagram.

subsystems.name: Molecular annotation
subsystems.role: label what kind of cell each neuron is and how each synapse behaves.

subsystems.name: Functional-state capture
subsystems.role: record the activity that carries moment-to-moment information and memory.

subsystems.name: Emulation
subsystems.role: run the reconstructed network as a working model.

subsystems.name: Validation and embodiment
subsystems.role: test whether the model behaves anything like the original.

buildSteps.title: Preserve the tissue
buildSteps.detail: A brain is chemically fixed and embedded so that membranes and synapses do not decay. Every current route to a connectome is destructive and post-mortem; no method can read a living human brain at this resolution.

buildSteps.title: Section and image
buildSteps.detail: The tissue is cut into thousands of ultra-thin slices, each imaged by electron microscopy at a few nanometres per pixel. A human brain at this resolution is an exabyte-scale dataset, far beyond anything produced today.

buildSteps.title: Align the slices
buildSteps.detail: Software stitches the images into one coherent three-dimensional volume, correcting for stretching, folds and knife marks.

buildSteps.title: Trace the wiring
buildSteps.detail: Machine-learning models segment each neuron and follow its branches; annotators then correct the errors. The result is a graph of cells and their connections.

buildSteps.title: Annotate cells and synapses
buildSteps.detail: Each neuron is assigned a type from molecular data, and each synapse gets properties such as whether it excites or inhibits.

buildSteps.title: Capture the dynamics
buildSteps.detail: This is the deepest unsolved step: structure alone does not record the strength of every synapse or the electrical state of the network. Activity recordings would have to be combined with the anatomy, and much human memory is known to be stored in dynamic, not static, form.

buildSteps.title: Simulate the network
buildSteps.detail: The graph is loaded into a simulator that steps each neuron through time. Matching a human brain's 86 billion neurons and roughly 100 trillion synapses in real time needs computing power well beyond current machines.

buildSteps.title: Validate against the original
buildSteps.detail: The emulation is given the same stimuli the person received and its responses compared. Only if it reproduces behaviour reliably would the claim of 'uploading a mind' even be testable.

buildSteps.title: Address the copy problem
buildSteps.detail: Even a perfect model is a reproduction, not a transfer. Nothing in this route moves a consciousness; it builds a second one, and whether that second one is a person is a question physics and biology cannot settle.

prerequisites.why: complete connectomes exist for a worm and, since 2024, an adult fruit fly; a human brain is orders of magnitude larger.

prerequisites.tech: Automated segmentation of dense neural tissue
prerequisites.why: proofreading still consumes enormous human effort even for small brains.

prerequisites.tech: Understanding of how neural activity encodes information
prerequisites.why: we can read broad patterns but not yet reconstruct the exact state of a network from its structure.

prerequisites.tech: Models that reproduce behaviour from a wiring diagram
prerequisites.why: no emulation of a real brain has yet produced behaviour matching the original animal.
the largest simulations today model fractions of a brain for short simulated times, far from real time.

pathway.milestone: complete connectomes of small animals and millimetre-scale fragments of mouse cortex, plus multi-modal maps combining wiring with gene expression
pathway.unlocks: methods for scaling up and for linking structure to cell type.

pathway.milestone: a whole mouse brain connectome with matched activity recordings
pathway.unlocks: the first realistic test of whether structure plus dynamics is enough to predict behaviour.

pathway.milestone: emulations of small circuits that reproduce learned behaviours
pathway.unlocks: confidence that a wiring diagram can be run as a functioning model.
speculative — a digital copy whose consciousness, identity and legal status would be entirely unresolved.
